ground_truth: Well, you're honing in on two things I've been thinking a lot about in the last 12 months, but certainly as for 27 years, I'll say long term is probably one of the concepts that we hold dearest. And that comes as much from being passed down from investors in our family. And our dad invested for us as kids. So we got the account and we could see what the returns were. And thank heavens he held the Washington Post for all those years. It helped pay for going to college. So we saw the benefits of it right there as young investors. And then diversification, I would say we're Motley at the Motley Fool. So we do have we do have members and we do have advisors and analysts who run more concentrated portfolios. I'm particularly a fan of diversification. And I'll highlight two reasons, although I probably have 24, but we don't want me to do that. The first is it's a wonderful way to learn about the world. So the father son team of Walter and Edwin Schloss, who were money managers, Buffett, was, I believe, in Benjamin Graham's classroom with the elder. And the Schloss approach was whenever we see anything interesting at all, we immediately buy shares because we know if we have skin in the game, we'll start following it. And we know the way the human mind works, that even though it's a small position, we'll almost start, you know, thinking about it as frequently as a large position. And what we don't want to do, let's make it contemporary. What we don't want to do is miss out on gene editing or machine learning and artificial intelligence or, or SAS when it's emerging with Salesforce or whatever is the next trend. We don't want to look at it, recoil or be protective of the companies that we have. We want to jump out and learn about the world. So that would be one reason for diversification. The second reason is that if you diversify, and we, there's many ways to define what diversification is, but let's just say 30 stocks. Once you have 30 stocks or 30 investments, you can then actually increase the risk. I'd say after your 20th position. So if you, if you open 23% positions, let's just say the next 10, you could, you can amp up the risk a little bit in those. And those open some alternative investments, some things that large wealth management firms aren't going to present because they look kind of absurd. They're not stable, you know, dividend paying, been around for decades. They're Fiverr with two R's on the end. No, we're not going to recommend that and put that in our client accounts. That would be embarrassing to the firm, you know, to the, to the brand that we've built up for decades. So to me, the beauty of diversification, second beauty is we're getting to learn a lot about the world. And the second is we can actually start to, as I Al Kusner on our staff says, we, we can, we can lean into the risk and then diversify the heck out of it. So again, if we, if we go endlessly far, okay, we just become an index fund. But if we have some constraint that we're looking for great long-term companies, and we're going to let our winners run, in fact, we're going to add money to our winners. So we'll, we'll just naturally penetrate our portfolio over time.

ground_truth: Well, it starts with data. And so when we look back and there's an Arizona State University study that that that that presents that over the last hundred years, 86 companies make up half of the stock market's capitalization and really one in 25 stocks are driving the vast majority of the equity returns. And so what we want to do is find that one in 25. And we know that over rolling 10 year periods, about 2 percent of all public companies will rise 10x and hold that 10x. So not a temporary GameStop, but a more legitimate, sustainable business that's being built successfully in the public market. So that's 2 percent. So it's one in one in 50. And so if we find that, the last thing we want to do is let it go, because that's going to have the potential to drive a substantial amount of our of our long term returns. Obviously, there are tax implications to holding. And if you're in an IRA or 401k self-directed, you maybe can be a little bit more active. But I think the data is is really what drives us there. But what we did was did a historical study of the data and we found some interesting things. I'll just share three of them. The first is if we had never sold a stock, we would have better returns because all it takes is selling 120 X return too soon. And all of the smart sales you made on companies that didn't succeed, they're not going to add up to that to that that enormous 20 bagger. So that's that's one. Number two, we found that those members historically who had purchased 30 random selections of our recommendations and held them for five years looking backwards. Now we do have the financial crisis and the pandemic. So we have some good data in these 18 years. Looking back over those 18 years, if you had done that 30 random stocks, five year holding period, you had a ninety seven point six percent chance of making money. And for many people, when they start investing, that's really that's their that's their primary ask. We all, as we get better and more interested, love the subject, want to improve our returns and hopefully do better than average. But for the majority of people who might start buying stocks, they want to make money. And so I think that five year data diversification. Sets them up for the probabilities in their favor. There are no certainties.
